Active scalar φ⁴ theories studied include both nonconserved (Model A) and conserved (Model B) dynamics.
These active models break time-reversal symmetry via active chemical potential terms.
Activity is irrelevant in the renormalization group sense near the liquid-vapor critical point.
Despite RG irrelevance, the singular part of the entropy production rate per spacetime correlation volume remains finite or diverges near criticality.
The steady-state entropy production rate (EPR) is decomposed into three terms proportional to active couplings λ and κ.
The natural scaling of EPR near criticality is σ ∼ ξ^{-(d+z)} where ξ is correlation length and z is dynamic exponent.
At the Gaussian fixed point, the reduced entropy production exponent θ_σ = 0, indicating natural scaling.
Near the Wilson-Fisher fixed point in 4−ε dimensions, θ_σ = ν ε / 12 + O(ε²), which is positive, indicating enhanced entropy production.
The active coupling constants λ and κ flow to zero under RG but still influence entropy production scaling.
The entropy production rate vanishes identically in passive equilibrium systems due to time-reversal symmetry.
The calculation involves perturbative one-loop RG analysis and dimensional regularization.
Composite operators of dimension 8 with 4 fields contribute to the critical scaling of entropy production.
The dynamic exponent z and field scaling dimension χ satisfy z = d + 2χ for Model B and z = d + 2 + 2χ for Model A.
The critical exponent ν for correlation length is ν = 1/2 + ε/12 + O(ε²) near the Wilson-Fisher fixed point.
Entropy production may exhibit fractal or anomalous scaling across spatial scales between microscopic cutoff and correlation length.
Negative values of EPR are not excluded in critical parts due to subtraction of large positive microscopic contributions.
The study motivates numerical simulations of entropy production near criticality in active matter.
The models studied fall within the dynamic Ising universality class despite activity.
The results challenge the notion that active models become effectively passive at critical points.
The paper uses stochastic thermodynamics and Harada-Sasa type integral relations to express EPR.
